---
title: "Examples to help you decide"
---

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(binwise)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 8, fig.height = 5,
                     out.width = "100%", dpi = 120)
options(width = 80, digits = 4)
```

There is no single answer to whether a variable should be binned. These
examples show why. Each uses data included with binwise, so you can run it
without finding or preparing another dataset.

Read the explanation before the code, then compare your output with the plot.
The conclusions apply to these examples. They are questions to bring to your
own data, rather than rules that automatically choose bins for you.

[Download the R code for these examples](../examples/gallery.R).

## Zero can describe a different situation

In this fictional participation measure, zero means no participation.
Positive values describe how much someone participates. A separate zero
category preserves that distinction.

```{r meaningful-zero}
data("binwise_zero", package = "binwise")
zero_groups <- bin_diagnose(
  binwise_zero, "score", bins = 3, separate_zero = TRUE, warn = FALSE
)
zero_groups$bins[, c("bin", "lower", "upper", "n")]
```

**What to take from this.** Zero has meaning here because of how the variable
is defined. A large pile of zeros in another dataset may have a different
explanation. Even here, the positive scores do not automatically need bins.
[Work through this example step by step](first-steps.html).

## Equal counts can hide a wide range

This simulated trade-like share contains many small values and a few much
larger ones. Four groups with similar counts put a wide range of values in
the last group. Adding boundaries among the largest observations makes that
range easier to inspect.

```{r long-tail}
data("binwise_tail", package = "binwise")
tail_choices <- bin_compare(
  binwise_tail, "share", methods = "quantile",
  custom_breaks = list(more_detail = as.numeric(quantile(
    binwise_tail$share, c(0, .5, .75, .9, .95, .99, 1)
  )))
)
plot(
  tail_choices, type = "boundaries", show_counts = TRUE,
  value_format = "percent", xlab = "Share",
  main = "Similar counts can hide very different values",
  scheme_labels = c(quantile_4 = "Four groups", more_detail = "More detail at the top")
)
```

**What to take from this.** Look at ranges and counts together. Adding groups
can reveal differences among large values, but it also leaves fewer observations
in each group. A long tail is a reason to inspect your choices, not a reason
that the variable must be binned.

## Groups can hide a steady change

In this example, the outcome rises steadily with exposure. We know that because
we wrote the rule used to simulate the data. Four categories turn that steady
increase into four flat steps.

```{r smooth-change}
data("binwise_smooth", package = "binwise")
four_groups <- bin_diagnose(binwise_smooth, "exposure", bins = 4)
smooth_fit <- bin_interact(
  binwise_smooth, outcome = "outcome", variables = "exposure",
  schemes = list(four_groups = four_groups)
)
plot(smooth_fit, xlab = "Exposure", main = "Grouping hides change within each interval")
```

The `continuous` line uses the original numbers. `four_groups` uses the
categories. The shaded areas are 95% confidence intervals for the estimated
mean outcome, not ranges containing 95% of individual outcomes.

**What to take from this.** If the amount of exposure matters, these groups
throw away useful differences. The fact that a flat step crosses the line
near the middle of a group is not evidence that binning is appropriate.

## A curve is also worth comparing

A straight line can miss a relationship that bends. In this version of the
example, outcomes are higher at both ends of the exposure range. We keep the
same simulated noise and change the rule for the mean outcome.

```{r curved-change}
curved <- binwise_smooth
noise <- curved$outcome - curved$expected_outcome
curved$outcome <- 2 + .008 * (curved$exposure - 50)^2 + noise
curve_groups <- bin_diagnose(curved, "exposure", bins = 4)
curve_fit <- bin_interact(
  curved, outcome = "outcome", variables = "exposure",
  schemes = list(four_groups = curve_groups), spline_df = 3
)
plot(curve_fit, xlab = "Exposure", main = "Give the numeric model room to bend")
```

The `spline` model fits a smooth curve while keeping exposure as numbers.
`spline_df = 3` sets how much flexibility that curve has. It is a choice to
check, rather than a setting that is best for every dataset.

**What to take from this.** Categories can improve on a straight line simply
because the line has the wrong shape. Compare the groups with a curve too.
The [curve comparison guide](flexible-continuous.html) also checks predictions
for observations left out of fitting.

## A known jump can make groups useful

Here the simulated mean outcome jumps at zero. Within each side, further
changes in `x` do not change that mean when the other predictors are fixed.
This gives us a reason to try two groups before looking at prediction scores.

The example also includes `z`. The size of the jump changes with `z`, which is
what an interaction represents. Another variable, `control`, is included in
each model so the comparison uses the same additional information.

```{r known-jump, fig.height=5.5}
data("binwise_interaction", package = "binwise")
jump_groups <- bin_diagnose(
  binwise_interaction, "x", method = "custom",
  breaks = c(min(binwise_interaction$x), 0, max(binwise_interaction$x))
)
jump_fit <- bin_interact(
  binwise_interaction, outcome = "threshold_outcome",
  variables = c("x", "z"), controls = "control",
  schemes = list(two_groups = jump_groups)
)
plot(jump_fit, xlab = "Distance from the boundary",
     main = "Two groups can represent a known jump")
```

Each panel holds `z` at a different value. The straight-line model spreads
change across `x`. The grouped model can represent the jump.

Now compare predictions on observations left out of model fitting. The code
divides the data into five parts, fits each model using four parts, and predicts
the part left out. It repeats this until every observation has a prediction
from a model that was fitted without it.

```{r test-the-jump}
jump_check <- bin_validate(
  binwise_interaction, outcome = "threshold_outcome",
  variables = c("x", "z"), controls = "control",
  schemes = list(two_groups = list(x = list(breaks = c(-Inf, 0, Inf)))),
  spline_df = 3, reference = "spline", folds = 5, seed = 12, reps = 199
)
jump_check$scores
```

Look at **RMSE**, a summary of prediction error in the outcome's units. Lower
is better. In this example it is about 1.34 for the straight-line interaction,
1.28 for the curve model, and 1.20 for the two groups.

**What to take from this.** These bins have a known boundary, represent the
simulated relationship, and predict better than both alternatives in this
comparison. That is stronger evidence than looking at where fitted lines
cross. In real research, a jump has to be justified by the setting and the
evidence; this simulation does not establish a threshold in anyone else's data.

## A boundary can matter even when nobody equals zero

Here, negative changes are declines and positive changes are increases.
There are no exact zeros. If direction is the question, two groups can be
useful even though their counts differ.

```{r direction}
data("binwise_mixed", package = "binwise")
direction_choices <- bin_compare(
  binwise_mixed, "change", methods = "quantile",
  custom_breaks = list(direction = c(min(binwise_mixed$change), 0,
                                     max(binwise_mixed$change)))
)
plot(
  direction_choices, type = "boundaries", show_counts = TRUE,
  xlab = "Change", main = "Keep declines and increases separate",
  scheme_labels = c(quantile_4 = "Four groups", direction = "Boundary at zero")
)
```

**What to take from this.** Similar group sizes are not always the goal.
If direction matters, the boundary at zero preserves it. If the amount of
change matters too, two groups still hide information. With the package's
interval rule, a future exact zero would join the lower group.

## Bring the questions back to your data

What does each boundary mean? What differences disappear within a group?
Are there enough observations to make the comparison you want? If prediction
matters, do the groups help when tested on observations left out of fitting?

The [working-paper example](working-paper.html) brings these questions to
real trade and sanctions data. For datasets supplied with R and a guide to
related packages, see [real data and related work](real-data-and-related-work.html).
